lessons.title: Start Values with DATA
intro: DATA puts values into variables before the program even starts: DATA K / 3, 1, 4, 1 / fills the array K. The values are compiled right into the program, so no cards have to be read.
One DATA card can fill several variables: DATA X, Y / 2.5, 7.0 /. A star repeats a value: DATA A / 5*0.0 / sets five elements to zero.
DATA is for constants and starting tables: prices, conversion factors, names of months.

exercises.prompt: When does DATA put its values into the variables?
exercises.explanation: DATA values are part of the compiled program.

exercises.prompt: What does DATA A / 4*1.0 / do for DIMENSION A(4)?
Start N at 10 and X at 0.5.
exercises.explanation: The values go in the same order as the names.
The DATA values fill K(1), K(2), K(3) in order.

exercises.prompt: When is READ better than DATA?
options: When the values change from run to run
exercises.explanation: DATA is fixed in the program. Changing values belong on data cards.

exercises.prompt: Which is a good use for DATA?
options: The number of days in each month
exercises.explanation: Things that never change are perfect for DATA.

lessons.title: Sharing with COMMON
intro: Passing the same five values to every subroutine gets tedious. COMMON puts variables into a shared area of memory that every program unit can see.
COMMON RATE, TAX in the main program and COMMON R, T in a subroutine point to the same two places. They're matched by position, not by name: R is RATE, T is TAX.
That's powerful and risky: if two units list the variables in a different order, they quietly mix them up.

exercises.prompt: How are COMMON variables matched between program units?
options: By their position in the list
exercises.explanation: The first name in one COMMON is the first name in the other, whatever they're called.
In SHOW, B is the first COMMON position (the main program's A = 1.0) and A is the second (2.0).

exercises.prompt: Let the subroutine see the main program's TAX.
exercises.explanation: The same COMMON in both units makes TAX shared.

exercises.prompt: Why can COMMON cause hard-to-find bugs?
options: A unit with the names in a different order mixes up the values
exercises.explanation: Nothing checks the names. Many teams kept one COMMON card and copied it exactly into every subprogram.

exercises.prompt: When is an argument better than COMMON?
options: When the value is only needed by one or two subroutines
exercises.explanation: Arguments make it clear what goes in and out. COMMON is for things many units share.

exercises.prompt: What did a typical big FORTRAN program keep in COMMON?
options: Shared constants and tables, like physical constants or the state of a simulation
exercises.explanation: Weather and engineering programs kept their whole model in COMMON blocks.

lessons.title: A Bigger Program
intro: Real FORTRAN programs had hundreds of cards. The way to keep them under control: a short main program that calls subprograms, each doing one clear job.
The main program reads like a table of contents: read the data, compute, print the report. Each subprogram can be tested on its own, and fixed without touching the rest.
This idea, breaking a problem into small named parts, is still the heart of programming today.

exercises.prompt: In a well-built program, what does the main program mostly do?
options: Call the subprograms in the right order
exercises.explanation: Like a table of contents: the details live in the subprograms.

exercises.prompt: In the example, who calls AVG?
Why is FLOAT(N) used in AVG?
options: N is an integer, and the average needs a real division

exercises.prompt: What is the big advantage of small subprograms?
options: Each can be tested and fixed on its own
They use fewer cards in total
exercises.explanation: A bug in AVG is found and fixed in AVG, without touching the rest.

exercises.prompt: Stack the cards for a main program that calls HELLO, plus the subroutine.
exercises.explanation: Main program first, ending with its END, then the subroutine with its own END.

exercises.prompt: How many END cards does a deck with a main program and two subprograms have?
exercises.explanation: Every program unit ends with its own END card.
